concepts.title: What is a Graph?
concepts.contentHtml:
A graph is a set of vertices (points) connected by edges (lines). That's it!

Graphs model relationships: people connected by friendships, cities connected by roads, web pages connected by links.

Key vocabulary:

• Degree of a vertex: number of edges touching it
• Path: a sequence of edges connecting two vertices
• Connected: every pair of vertices has a path between them

concepts.title: The Handshaking Lemma
concepts.contentHtml:
The Handshaking Lemma: the sum of all vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges.

Why? Each edge contributes 1 to the degree of each of its two endpoints.

Consequence: the number of vertices with odd degree must be even. (Try it! You can't draw a graph where exactly 3 vertices have odd degree.)

This simple observation is surprisingly powerful for proving impossibility results.

concepts.title: Special Graphs
concepts.contentHtml:
Complete graph Kₙ: every pair of vertices is connected. K₃ is a triangle, K₄ has 6 edges, K₅ has 10.

Bipartite graph: vertices split into two groups, edges only between groups. Think of matching students to projects.

Tree: a connected graph with no cycles. n vertices, n-1 edges. Trees are the "most efficient" connected graphs.

Planar graph: can be drawn on a plane without edges crossing.

title: Eulerian & Hamiltonian Paths
description: Can you traverse every edge? Every vertex?

concepts.title: The Königsberg Bridge Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1736, Euler asked: can you walk through Königsberg crossing each bridge exactly once?

He proved it was impossible — and in doing so, invented graph theory.

An Eulerian path traverses every edge exactly once. An Eulerian circuit does so and returns to the start.

Euler's Theorem: An Eulerian circuit exists iff every vertex has even degree. An Eulerian path exists iff exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree.

concepts.title: Hamiltonian Paths
concepts.contentHtml:
A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex exactly once. A Hamiltonian cycle does so and returns to the start.

Unlike Euler paths, there is no simple criterion for when Hamiltonian paths exist. Checking is NP-complete — one of the hardest problems in computer science!

The Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP): find the shortest Hamiltonian cycle through a set of cities. It's NP-hard, and billions of dollars depend on approximate solutions (logistics, chip design, DNA sequencing).

concepts.title: Euler vs Hamilton Comparison
concepts.contentHtml:
A useful comparison:

Eulerian: Visit every edge once. Easy to check (degree condition). Polynomial-time algorithm.

Hamiltonian: Visit every vertex once. Hard to check. NP-complete.

The gap between these two similar-sounding problems is one of the great mysteries of computer science. It's closely related to the P vs NP problem — another Millennium Prize question!

title: Graph Coloring
description: How many colors do you need?

concepts.title: Vertex Coloring
concepts.contentHtml:
Graph coloring: assign colors to vertices so that no two adjacent vertices share a color.

The chromatic number χ(G) is the minimum number of colors needed.

χ(Kₙ) = n (complete graphs need one color per vertex).
χ(tree) = 2 (trees are always 2-colorable).
χ(cycle of even length) = 2, odd length = 3.

Practical use: scheduling! Courses that share students can't be at the same time — this is graph coloring.

concepts.title: The Four Color Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
The Four Color Theorem: every planar graph can be properly colored with at most 4 colors.

This means any map can be colored with 4 colors so that neighboring regions have different colors. Conjectured in 1852, proved in 1976 — the first major theorem proved by computer.

The proof checked 1,936 configurations by machine. This was controversial: can a proof no human can verify really be trusted? The debate shaped philosophy of mathematics.

concepts.title: Chromatic Polynomials
concepts.contentHtml:
The chromatic polynomial P(G, k) counts the number of proper colorings using at most k colors.

For a complete graph: P(Kₙ, k) = k(k-1)(k-2)...(k-n+1).

For a tree with n vertices: P(T, k) = k(k-1)ⁿ⁻¹.

These polynomials encode deep structural information about the graph and connect graph theory to algebra.

title: Trees, Networks, & Algorithms
description: Spanning trees, shortest paths, and real-world networks

concepts.title: Spanning Trees
concepts.contentHtml:
A spanning tree of a graph G is a tree that includes all vertices and is a subgraph of G.

Every connected graph has a spanning tree (possibly many). A minimum spanning tree (MST) minimizes total edge weight.

Kruskal's algorithm: sort edges by weight, greedily add the lightest edge that doesn't create a cycle.
Prim's algorithm: grow the tree one edge at a time, always choosing the cheapest connection to a new vertex.

MSTs are used in network design, clustering, and circuit wiring.

concepts.title: Shortest Paths
concepts.contentHtml:
Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted graph (with non-negative weights).

It's a greedy algorithm: always extend the path to the nearest unvisited vertex.

Used by: GPS navigation, network routing, game AI pathfinding.

For graphs with negative edges, use Bellman-Ford. For all-pairs shortest paths, use Floyd-Warshall.

concepts.title: Real-World Networks
concepts.contentHtml:
Graph theory is the mathematics of networks:

Social networks: Small-world phenomenon — ~6 degrees of separation. Power-law degree distributions (few hubs, many low-degree nodes).

The internet: Routers as vertices, connections as edges. BGP routing is graph algorithms in real time.

Biology: Protein interaction networks, neural networks, food webs. Graph analysis reveals functional modules and vulnerabilities.

PageRank: Google's original algorithm models the web as a graph and ranks pages by the structure of incoming links (this connects back to eigenvalues!).
